title: Commented analyses of two real-world studies
text:
In this web extra to the manuscript The Problem with Univariable Selection in Regression Modelling-and What To Do Instead (Ullmann et al. 2026), we present reproducible analyses of two real-world case studies. For each case study, we first apply modelling strategies appropriate to the respective research question. We then contrast these results with those obtained using a univariable selection strategy, illustrating the implications of data-driven variable selection based on univariable screening. The analyses are intended as examples rather than comprehensive analyses of the underlying studies. Applied studies may require additional modelling steps depending on the research question and context. For comprehensive results and the full analyses, we refer readers to the original publications.
All analyses, tables, and figures reported in this web extra can be reproduced by running the accompanying R code.

Clicking on Code allows the reader to view the R code needed to recreate the analysis.

Green boxes contain additional explanations, which may include suggestions for further analyses that should be considered in an applied analysis.




Case studies



1
Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis  The aim was to investigate the prognostic relevance of PMP22 gene expression while accounting for established clinical predictors. The modelling objective was prediction. The example is based on the study of Tong et al. (2010).


2
A descriptive model for schoolchildren’s lung health  The aim was to identify variables most strongly associated with forced vital capacity in schoolchildren in a multivariable context, without necessarily implying that the observed associations are causal. The modelling objective was description. The example is based on Buchholz, Holländer, and Sauerbrei (2008).

title: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
This example is based on the study of Tong et al. (2010). Previous work suggested that gene expression of peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) differs between invasive and non-invasive breast cell lines. Therefore, Tong et al. investigated its prognostic relevance in breast cancer using a retrospective multicentre study. PMP22 gene expression and clinical variables were measured in primary breast tumors by real-time PCR. The aim was to evaluate the association between PMP22 and prognosis while accounting for established clinical predictors: nodal status, estrogen receptor status, tumour size, and tumour grade. The modelling objective was prediction.
The PMP22 data are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19632791 (Heinze and Tong 2026) and include a data dictionary.
The original publication reports 249 patients. However, the publicly available dataset contains 248 observations. Therefore, analyses are based on the available 248 patients.

1.1 Data preparation
Required packages are loaded and helper functions defined.

# helper: extract HR, 95% CI, p-value, n and number of events from a
# fitted Cox model, one row per coefficient; reused throughout the paper
extract_cox <- function(fit) {
  s <- summary(fit)
  data.frame(
    variable = rownames(s$coefficients),
    n        = fit$n,
    events   = s$nevent,
    HR       = s$coefficients[, "exp(coef)"],
    CI_low   = s$conf.int[, "lower .95"],
    CI_high  = s$conf.int[, "upper .95"],
    p        = s$coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
  )
}

1.2 Data dictionary
The analysis-ready data set (pmpdata) contains the following variables:

1.2.1 Outcome

days: Follow-up time (in days) from diagnosis to recurrence, death, or end of follow-up, whichever occurred first

rezs: Event indicator (1 = recurrence or death; 0 = censored or cancer-unrelated death)



1.2.2 Predictors

PMP22: Peripheral myelin protein 22 (0 = negative, 1 = positive)

pT: Tumour size (1 = pT1 <1 cm, 2 = pT2 2-5 cm, 3 = pT3 >5 cm or pT4)

pN: Nodal status (0 = pN0, 1 = pN1)

G: Tumour grade (1 = G1, 2 = G2, 3 = G3)

ER: Estrogen receptor status (0 = negative, 1 = positive)

Factor variables (with suffix _f) provide labelled versions for presentation.
The complete-case dataset (pmpdata_complete) excludes observations with missing values. Of the 248 patients, 208 are included in the complete-case analysis.

1.5 Main research question
The objective is to estimate the association between PMP22 and disease-free survival while adjusting for established clinical predictors. A multivariable Cox model is specified a priori. No data-driven variable selection is applied.






Additional information: model considerations





In applied analyses, key assumptions of the Cox model should be assessed, including proportional hazards and potential multicollinearity. Pre-specified interactions may be considered where clinically justified. If the proportional hazards assumption is violated (e.g., for ER), time-varying effects can be incorporated, for example, by modelling an interaction of ER with log(days).

2.1 Univariable screening
Each model is fitted on the subset of data available for that predictor. Consequently, sample size and number of events can vary across models. This is often not reported.


Code
vars <- c("PMP22", "pT", "pN", "G", "ER")

# fit one univariable Cox model per candidate predictor, each using whatever
# observations happen to be non-missing for that single variable
uni_fits <- lapply(vars, function(v) {
  coxph(as.formula(paste0("Surv(days, rezs) ~ ", v)), data = pmpdata, na.action = na.omit)
})
names(uni_fits) <- vars

uni_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(uni_fits, extract_cox))

uni_display <- uni_tab %>%
  transmute(
    Variable = variable,
    n = n,
    Events = events,
    HR = round(HR, 2),
    `p-value` = format.pval(p, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
  )

uni_display <- uni_tab %>%
  transmute(
    Variable = factor(variable, levels = vars),
    `n (events)` = paste0(n, " (", events, ")"),
    HR = round(HR, 2),
    `95% CI` = paste0("(", round(CI_low, 2), ", ", round(CI_high, 2), ")"),
    `p-value` = format.pval(p, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
  ) %>%
  arrange(Variable)

alpha_screen <- 0.05

selected <- uni_tab$variable[uni_tab$p < alpha_screen]
dropped <- setdiff(vars, selected)

Only nodal status (pN) and estrogen receptor status (ER) are selected by univariable screening. PMP22, the variable of primary interest, is excluded. This occurs because univariable associations do not account for confounding. The effect of PMP22 (PMP22) is masked by its correlation with ER status (ER), which becomes apparent only after adjustment.

Additional information: interpretation after selection





Estimates from a model derived via variable selection are typically reported as if the selected variables had been pre-specified. However, standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values do not account for the selection process and are therefore biased, i.e., typically they are too optimistic. In practice, this limitation is often not acknowledged and the application of univariable screening is sometimes not reported.

title: A descriptive model for schoolchildren’s lung health
text:
We reanalyse data from a German study on the effects of ozone exposure on schoolchildren’s lung growth, conducted between 1996 and 1999 (Ihorst et al. 2004). Following Buchholz, Holländer, and Sauerbrei (2008), we consider a subset of 496 children with complete data on 24 variables potentially associated with the continuous outcome forced vital capacity in litres, measured in autumn 1997. The data are publicly available in the code supplement of Sauerbrei et al. (2014) (https://doi.org/10.1002/bimj.201300222).
Our goal was descriptive modelling. We aimed to identify the variables most strongly associated with forced vital capacity in a multivariable context, without necessarily implying that the identified associations are causal.
In this analysis, the pre-specified full model is contrasted with a multivariable model derived via univariable selection and a second multivariable model derived via backward elimination with AIC.

Required packages are loaded and helper functions defined.

# helper: extract point estimates, 95% Wald CIs and p-values from a fitted
# lm (or abe) model, one row per coefficient
extract_lm <- function(fit) {
  cf <- summary(fit)$coefficients
  data.frame(
    variable = rownames(cf),
    beta     = cf[, 1],
    CI_low   = cf[, 1] - qnorm(0.975) * cf[, 2],
    CI_high  = cf[, 1] + qnorm(0.975) * cf[, 2],
    p        = cf[, 4]
  )
}

Additional information: low prevalences





Such low prevalences give few informative observations for these covariates, which can make the corresponding coefficient estimates imprecise and unstable in the models that follow. In an applied analysis, this has to be accounted for, for example by:

Interpreting the estimated associations for rare covariates cautiously, emphasising the width of the confidence interval rather than the point estimate.
Checking, via leverage/influence diagnostics, whether the few observations in the rare category disproportionately drive the estimated association.
Combining a rare category with a conceptually related, more prevalent one, but only where this is clinically and scientifically sensible, not merely to increase cell counts.

This comparison is descriptive and post hoc, not a formal statistical test between models: apparent R^2 never decreases as covariates are added and so favours larger models regardless of whether the added covariates are truly relevant. Adjusted R^2 and AIC both penalise the number of parameters and thus give a fairer, if still informal, comparison of fit against parsimony across models of different size. For AIC, smaller values indicate the preferred trade-off between fit and complexity.
Although the model based on univariable selection includes fewer covariates, it explains only slightly less variance than the much larger full model. Apparent R^2 alone cannot distinguish a well-specified model from one that has excluded relevant covariates.
Although neither the full model nor the backward-elimination model can be assumed to represent the true data-generating process, this example illustrates why univariable screening can be problematic: marginal associations do not reliably determine which variables are relevant once covariates are considered jointly.







Key message



Marginal (univariable) associations do not reliably indicate which variables matter once other covariates are taken into account. Univariable selection excluded high_ozone and wheeze, both of which showed a clear association with FFVC in the full model (masking), while retaining variables such as age and birth_weight whose univariable associations were attenuated once correlated covariates such as height and weight were included in the model (amplification). Backward elimination with AIC, which considers all covariates jointly at every step, produced a model closer to the full model and did not exclude high_ozone or wheeze.









What would be done in a real analysis?



This worked example is simplified. A full best-practice analysis would additionally include:

Define the modelling objective (here: descriptive) before looking at the data, and decide a priori, based on subject-matter knowledge, which covariates define the starting set, the full model.
Decide whether data-driven variable selection is reasonable at all in the given setting, based on the modelling aim (e.g., descriptive vs. predictive) and on whether the sample size or events-per-variable ratio (model complexity) can support it.
Conduct a structured initial data analysis (IDA) before model specification, examining the distributions of the outcome and candidate covariates (e.g., outliers, implausible values, rare categories), missing-data patterns, and multicollinearity or redundancy among candidate covariates (e.g., via pairwise correlations), as outlined in Heinze et al. (2024).
Limit the complexity of the final model to what the available sample size can support, for example by applying sample-size or events-per-variable considerations for the number of candidate predictor parameters (Harrell Jr. (2015), Heinze, Wallisch, and Dunkler (2018), Riley et al. (2019), Ullmann et al. (2026)), to reduce the risk of overfitting.
Examine functional forms for the continuous covariates (age, birth weight, height, NO2, O3, temperature, weight) rather than assuming linearity, e.g., using fractional polynomials as implemented in the mfp2 package (Kipruto et al. 2025).
Consider relevant interactions where scientifically plausible.
Examine residual diagnostics (e.g., residuals-versus-fitted and QQ-plots) and influence diagnostics (e.g., Cook’s distance) for both the full model and the final selected model(s), to check the linear-model assumptions and to identify observations that unduly affect the results.
If a data-driven selection procedure is used, quantify selection instability, e.g., through bootstrap inclusion frequencies (available in the abe package) (Blagus et al. 2025).
Assess predictive performance using resampling that repeats the entire modelling process, including any variable-selection step, within each resample.
Report effect estimates with confidence intervals rather than relying on p-values alone.

title: A descriptive model for schoolchildren’s lung health
text:
We reanalyse data from a German study on the effects of ozone exposure on schoolchildren’s lung growth, conducted between 1996 and 1999 (Ihorst et al. 2004). Following Buchholz, Holländer, and Sauerbrei (2008), we consider a subset of 496 children with complete data on 24 variables potentially associated with the continuous outcome forced vital capacity in litres, measured in autumn 1997. The data are publicly available in the code supplement of Sauerbrei et al. (2014) (https://doi.org/10.1002/bimj.201300222).
Our goal was descriptive modelling. We aimed to identify the variables most strongly associated with forced vital capacity in a multivariable context, without necessarily implying that the identified associations are causal.
In this analysis, the pre-specified full model is contrasted with a multivariable model derived via univariable selection and a second multivariable model derived via backward elimination with AIC.

Additional information: low prevalences





Such low prevalences give few informative observations for these covariates, which can make the corresponding coefficient estimates imprecise and unstable in the models that follow. In an applied analysis, this has to be accounted for, for example by:

Interpreting the estimated associations for rare covariates cautiously, emphasising the width of the confidence interval rather than the point estimate.
Checking, via leverage/influence diagnostics, whether the few observations in the rare category disproportionately drive the estimated association.
Combining a rare category with a conceptually related, more prevalent one, but only where this is clinically and scientifically sensible, not merely to increase cell counts.
Using estimation methods less sensitive to small cell counts (e.g., penalised/Firth-type regression, or bootstrap confidence intervals).
Reporting a sensitivity analysis that excludes rare covariates, to check whether conclusions for the remaining covariates depend on their inclusion.

This comparison is descriptive and post hoc, not a formal statistical test between models: apparent R^2 never decreases as covariates are added and so favours larger models regardless of whether the added covariates are truly relevant. Adjusted R^2 and AIC both penalise the number of parameters and thus give a fairer, if still informal, comparison of fit against parsimony across models of different size. For AIC, smaller values indicate the preferred trade-off between fit and complexity.
Although the model based on univariable selection includes fewer covariates, it explains only slightly less variance than the much larger full model. Apparent R^2 alone cannot distinguish a well-specified model from one that has excluded relevant covariates.
Although neither the full model nor the backward-elimination model can be assumed to represent the true data-generating process, this example illustrates why univariable screening can be problematic: marginal associations do not reliably determine which variables are relevant once covariates are considered jointly.







Key message



Marginal (univariable) associations do not reliably indicate which variables matter once other covariates are taken into account. Univariable selection excluded high_ozone and wheeze, both of which showed a clear association with FFVC in the full model (masking), while retaining variables such as age and birth_weight whose univariable associations were attenuated once correlated covariates such as height and weight were included in the model (amplification). Backward elimination with AIC, which considers all covariates jointly at every step, produced a model closer to the full model and did not exclude high_ozone or wheeze.









What would be done in a real analysis?



This worked example is simplified. A full best-practice analysis would additionally include:

Define the modelling objective (here: descriptive) before looking at the data, and decide a priori, based on subject-matter knowledge, which covariates define the starting set, the full model.
Decide whether data-driven variable selection is reasonable at all in the given setting, based on the modelling aim (e.g., descriptive vs. predictive) and on whether the sample size or events-per-variable ratio (model complexity) can support it.
Conduct a structured initial data analysis (IDA) before model specification, examining the distributions of the outcome and candidate covariates (e.g., outliers, implausible values, rare categories), missing-data patterns, and multicollinearity or redundancy among candidate covariates (e.g., via pairwise correlations), as outlined in Heinze et al. (2024).
Limit the complexity of the final model to what the available sample size can support, for example by applying sample-size or events-per-variable considerations for the number of candidate predictor parameters (Harrell Jr. (2015), Heinze, Wallisch, and Dunkler (2018), Riley et al. (2019), Ullmann et al. (2026)), to reduce the risk of overfitting.
Examine functional forms for the continuous covariates (age, birth weight, height, NO2, O3, temperature, weight) rather than assuming linearity, e.g., using fractional polynomials as implemented in the mfp2 package (Kipruto et al. 2025).
Consider relevant interactions where scientifically plausible.
Examine residual diagnostics (e.g., residuals-versus-fitted and QQ-plots) and influence diagnostics (e.g., Cook’s distance) for both the full model and the final selected model(s), to check the linear-model assumptions and to identify observations that unduly affect the results.
If a data-driven selection procedure is used, quantify selection instability, e.g., through bootstrap inclusion frequencies (available in the abe package) (Blagus et al. 2025).
Assess predictive performance using resampling that repeats the entire modelling process, including any variable-selection step, within each resample.
Report effect estimates with confidence intervals rather than relying on p-values alone.

title: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
This example is based on the study of Tong et al. (2010). Previous work suggested that gene expression of peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) differs between invasive and non-invasive breast cell lines. Therefore, Tong et al. investigated its prognostic relevance in breast cancer using a retrospective multicentre study. PMP22 gene expression and clinical variables were measured in primary breast tumors by real-time PCR. The aim was to evaluate the association between PMP22 and prognosis while accounting for established clinical predictors: nodal status, estrogen receptor status, tumour size, and tumour grade. The modelling objective was prediction.
The PMP22 data are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19632791 (Heinze and Tong 2026) and include a data dictionary.
The original publication reports 249 patients. However, the publicly available dataset contains 248 observations. Therefore, analyses are based on the available 248 patients.

# helper: extract HR, 95% CI, p-value, n and number of events from a
# fitted Cox model, one row per coefficient; reused throughout the paper
extract_cox <- function(fit) {
  s <- summary(fit)

    variable = rownames(s$coefficients),

Additional information: interpretation after selection





Estimates from a model derived via variable selection are typically reported as if the selected variables had been pre-specified. However, standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values do not account for the selection process and are therefore biased, i.e., typically they are too optimistic. In practice, this limitation is often not acknowledged and the application of univariable screening is sometimes not reported.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
Two contrasting Statistical Analysis Plans (SAP) for the same prediction problem are presented.

Section 1: A pre-specified multivariable strategy consistent with current best-practice guidance.
Section 2: A common but flawed workflow built on univariable variable selection.
Section 3: Comparison of both approaches.

Both operate on the same 248-patient dataset and the same disease-free survival outcome, so any difference in conclusions is attributable to the statistical strategy, not to the data.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
A.1 Objective
The objective is to estimate a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model for disease-free survival containing all five pre-specified predictors simultaneously, to quantify the (adjusted) prognostic contribution of PMP22 alongside established clinical factors, and to report its incremental and overall prediction performance. No predictor is excluded based on its own association with the outcome.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
A.2 Initial data analysis (IDA)
Before the analysis, an IDA is conducted to assess data quality and distributions and to adapt the SAP if data peculiarities warrant modifications.

Technical/range checks: valid coding of each factor (PMP22, pN, ER \in {0,1}; pT, G \in {1,2,3}); days > 0; consistency between days/rezs and plausible follow-up (no negative or implausibly short times without a corresponding early event).
Univariate distributions and cross-tabulations of all predictors (not against the outcome for selection purposes, but to check plausibility, e.g., expected positive correlation between PMP22 and ER as reported previously).
Missing-data description: missingness per variable, pattern, and proportion of cases with missing predictors.
Missing-data mechanism: compare observed-vs-missing subgroups on the other observed covariates and on the outcome (event indicator, log follow-up time) via logistic regression of each missingness indicator on the remaining variables, to assess plausibility of missing-at-random (MAR) vs missing-completely-at-random (MCAR). No formal test (e.g., Little’s MCAR) is decisive here. The assessment is used only to justify a potential imputation, not to change which variables are modeled. If missingness appears related to the unobserved value itself even after conditioning on the observed data (i.e., missing-not-at-random, MNAR, cannot be ruled out), no MNAR-specific modeling (e.g., pattern-mixture or selection models) is planned given the modest overall missingness (16.1% of cases); this is instead reported as a limitation of the multiple imputation-based primary analysis.
Outcome description: number of events (109), event rate (44.0%), median follow-up computed by the reverse Kaplan-Meier method (Schemper and Smith 1996).
Document the analysis population precisely (n = 248 vs. 249 in the original publication) and produce a simple flow description of excluded/available cases.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
A.3 Outcome handling

Disease-free survival analysis only: This working dataset does not contain age and overall survival, unlike the full published analysis.
Right-censoring assumed non-informative: This is an assumption, not something testable from these data, and should be stated explicitly as a limitation.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
A.4 Predictor specification
Fitting of the functional forms decided before data analysis

PMP22, pN, ER: binary, entered as 0/1 indicators. No functional-form issue.
pT, G: ordinal with 3 levels. Primary specification uses a linear (ordinal-score) coding (with 1 df each) reflecting the natural monotonic ordering (higher stage/grade \rightarrow worse prognosis is biologically plausible). Adequacy of this constraint is checked separately for pT and for G, via likelihood-ratio test (LRT) comparing the model with that variable linear-coded against the same model with only that variable recoded as a free 3-level factor (1 additional df), the other predictors held at their pre-specified form. A significance level of \alpha = 0.05 is pre-specified as the decision rule for each LRT: if p < 0.05, the free (categorical) coding is used for that variable instead; otherwise the more parsimonious linear coding is retained. This is a pre-specified functional form check, which is distinct from variable selection. No predictor is dropped. This check is performed before the main-effects model is finalized (A.6 Model-building strategy).
Full model has 5 (ordinal coding) to 7 (fully categorical pT/G) degrees of freedom. With 109 events, events-per-parameter is \approx 21.8 (linear coding) to \approx 15.6 (fully categorical), both within the EPV \geq 15 rule of thumb (Harrell Jr. 2015); note that modern sample-size guidance (e.g. Riley et al .) would be used prospectively for a new study but is reported here only as a plausibility check on an existing dataset.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
A.5 Missing data

Primary analysis: multiple imputation (MI) by chained equations / fully conditional specification for PMP22, pT, pN, G, ER, using all other predictors plus outcome information. For the outcome, follow White & Royston’s recommendation for imputing covariates in survival models (White and Royston 2009): include the Nelson-Aalen estimator of the cumulative baseline hazard and the event indicator rezs as predictors in the imputation model (rather than raw survival time), to avoid distorting the covariate-outcome associations.
Number of imputations: at least \approx 100 \times (fraction of incomplete cases) \approx 100 \times 0.161 \approx 16 (White, Royston & Wood rule of thumb) (White, Royston, and Wood 2011); use m = 20 - 50 for additional stability of pooled estimates and CIs.
Estimates pooled across imputations using Rubin’s rules for the Cox model coefficients, standard errors, and (where feasible) performance measures.
Sensitivity analysis: repeat the full-model analysis on complete cases only (n = 208) and compare coefficients/HRs qualitatively to the MI results.
Congeniality with the interaction model: the imputation model above includes only main effects, whereas A.7 Interaction (see below) pre-specifies interaction terms (PMP22\timesER, PMP22\timespN, PMP22\timespT). To keep the imputation congenial with this substantive model, the interaction terms are handled by passive imputation (formed as products of the already-imputed variables within each of the m completed datasets, rather than imputed directly as separate variables). As a check, the interaction analysis (A.7) is repeated on complete cases only, and any material discrepancy with the multiple imputation-based result is reported.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
A.6 Model-building strategy

Single, pre-specified Cox proportional hazards model with all five predictors entered as main effects simultaneously. No univariable pre-screening, no stepwise/backward elimination, no data-driven inclusion threshold, because the predictors were chosen a priori on clinical grounds and the modeling aim is prediction/adjustment, not discovery.
Multicollinearity check: pairwise associations among predictors (e.g. PMP22 and ER) and generalized variance inflation factors (GVIF, appropriate for categorical predictors) to confirm the design is not degenerate; no variable is removed unless GVIF indicates a practically unidentifiable model (e.g., GVIF^{1/(2\times df)} > 2, the categorical-predictor analogue of VIF > 4; not expected here given only five predictors, n = 248).
Analysis sequence: the order of steps is fixed a priori as (i) finalize the coding of pT and G via the pre-specified functional-form LRTs (A.4 Predictor specification) and fit the resulting main-effects model; (ii) check proportional-hazards assumptions on this model (A.8 Checking modeling assumptions), amending it if needed (e.g., adding a time-dependent term for ER); (iii) test the pre-specified interactions (A.7 Interactions) via the joint LRT against the (possibly amended) main-effects model. This order avoids interactions being tested against a model not yet checked for basic assumption violations, and avoids proportional-hazards checks being run on a model whose functional form is still unsettled.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
A.7 Interactions

Interactions are not searched exhaustively. A small, pre-specified, clinically motivated set is tested: PMP22 $\times$ ER (biologically plausible given their reported correlation and shared pathway relevance) and, secondarily, PMP22 $\times$ pN and PMP22 $\times$ pT (directly relevant to the study question of whether PMP22’s effect depends on classical tumor-spread markers).
A single joint LRT comparing the main-effects model to the model with all pre-specified product terms added is performed first, to protect against multiplicity from testing several interactions individually. Individual interaction terms are inspected only if the joint test is significant (\alpha = 0.05).
Given limited events-per-parameter, any retained interaction is treated as exploratory/hypothesis-generating; the primary reported prediction model remains the main-effects model unless an interaction is both statistically compelling and clinically sensible.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
A.8 Checking modeling assumptions

Proportional hazards: global and per-covariate tests based on scaled Schoenfeld residuals (Grambsch & Therneau test) plus a graphical check (smoothed residuals vs. time) (Grambsch and Therneau 1994). If a covariate (e.g., ER, as found in the source publication) shows a time-varying effect, this is accounted for with a time-dependent covariate (interaction with log(days)) or by stratification, and its impact on the other coefficients is reported.
Functional form: as described in A.4 (linear vs. ordinal coding for pT and G).
Influential observations: dfbeta/dfbetas per covariate to flag cases with disproportionate influence on individual coefficients; martingale and deviance residuals for overall fit. Consistent with the pre-specified, non-data-driven nature of this SAP, influential cases are reported and discussed but the model is not refitted after their removal; any such exercise, if performed, is clearly labeled as a post hoc sensitivity analysis.
Multicollinearity: as in A.6.
All checks performed on (and pooled/summarized across, where relevant) the imputed datasets, not only on a single complete-case fit.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
A.9 Quantifying prediction performance

Discrimination: Harrell’s C-index and/or Uno’s C (the latter uses inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting to target a population concordance measure up to a pre-specified truncation time \tau, e.g., 5 years, and is less biased than Harrell’s C under moderate-to-heavy or covariate-dependent censoring); time-dependent AUC(t) at clinically relevant horizons (e.g., 3 and 5 years).
Calibration: calibration plot of model-predicted vs. Kaplan-Meier observed disease-free survival probability at fixed horizons (e.g., 3-, 5-year), with calibration intercept and slope.
Overall/global accuracy: Schemper & Henderson’s explained variation V (Schemper and Henderson 2000) (directly comparable to the measure used in the source publication) and/or the (integrated) Brier score.
Internal validation: bootstrap resampling (B \approx 500 - 1000), Harrell’s optimism-correction approach applied to the C-index, calibration slope (shrinkage factor), and explained variation, rather than reporting apparent (in-sample) performance as final. 10-fold cross-validation, as used in the original publication, is an acceptable alternative but bootstrap optimism-correction is may be preferred for its lower variance with datasets of this size.
Combining the bootstrap with multiple imputation: the optimism correction is performed within each of the m imputed datasets separately (drawing B bootstrap samples from each completed dataset, refitting the full model-building and validation procedure in each, and computing optimism), rather than bootstrapping the stacked/completed data as if it were a single dataset. The resulting optimism-corrected estimates are then averaged (and their variances combined) across the m imputations using Rubin’s rules, so that imputation uncertainty is not lost in the resampling step.
Optional: relative importance of predictors via the “leave-one-out” explained-variation decomposition (Heinze and Schemper 2003), reported for interpretation only, not for selection.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
A.10 Conditional predicted survival curves

To make the model’s predictions concrete, conditional predicted disease-free survival curves are computed for one or more representative covariate profiles defined a priori. For each profile, the Cox model is used to estimate the predicted disease-free survival conditional on the specified values of all covariates (pT, pN, G, and ER), typically contrasting PMP22-high versus PMP22-low while keeping all other covariates fixed. This provides an interpretable patient-level illustration of the model predictions rather than presenting regression coefficients alone. Profiles should represent plausible and sufficiently populated combinations of covariates (e.g. common or clinically relevant categories) rather than extreme or sparsely observed combinations, to avoid predictions that rely on extrapolation beyond the support of the data.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
A.11 Reporting

Follow TRIPOD reporting guidance for a prediction model (Moons et al. 2015):

patient flow (249 \rightarrow 248 \rightarrow imputed/complete-case),
baseline characteristics table,
full table with hazard ratios (HR) (all five predictors) with 95% CIs from the pooled model,
proportional-hazards and functional-form diagnostics, discrimination and calibration figures (apparent and optimism-corrected), and
an explicit statement that no variable selection was performed.
Limitations, reported explicitly (TRIPOD item 20): (i) center (Vienna vs. Innsbruck) is not available in the working dataset, so multicenter clustering/heterogeneity cannot be assessed or adjusted for; (ii) only internal validation (bootstrap optimism-correction) is performed (no independent external validation cohort is available), so reported performance reflects internal validity only, not generalizability to other settings; (iii) right-censoring is assumed non-informative, which cannot be tested from these data (A.3 Outcome handling); (iv) the events-per-parameter assessment (A.4 Predictor specification) is a retrospective plausibility check on an existing dataset, not a prospective sample-size calculation; (v) missing-not-at-random cannot be excluded for pT, pN, G (A.2); (vi) age and overall survival, available in the original published analysis, are absent from this working dataset (A.3 Outcome handling).

Unadjusted Kaplan-Meier curves by PMP22 category may be shown for descriptive purposes, but explicitly labeled as potentially confounded (e.g,. by thePMP22-ER association) and not used to justify inclusion or exclusion of any predictor.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
B.1 Univariable screening

Fit a separate univariable Cox model (or log-rank test) for each candidate predictor (PMP22, pT, pN, G, ER) against disease-free survival, each using whatever cases happen to be non-missing for that single variable.
Pitfall: the analysis sample silently changes from test to test, which is rarely reported and makes results non-comparable.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
B.2 Apply a significance filter

Retain only variables with univariable p < 0.05. Some variants use relaxed thresholds, like p < 0.10 or 0.20, “to be safe”.
Potential pitfall: It is possible that the variable of primary interest is eliminated at this stage. Based on the univariable HRs reported in the source publication for disease-free survival (PMP22: HR 1.01, p = 0.978; pT: HR 1.32, p = 0.061; pN: HR 2.72, p < 0.0001; G: HR 1.06, p = 0.703; ER: HR 0.63, p = 0.017; the exact values for this 248-case dataset may differ slightly but the pattern is expected to be similar), this filter would drop PMP22 This directly defeats the study’s stated aim of evaluating PMP22 if established clinical factors are taken into consideration, since PMP22 never reaches the stage where it could be adjusted for those factors.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
section: B.3 Multivariable model on the surviving subset
text:
B.3 Multivariable model on the surviving subset

Fit a Cox model with only the variables that passed B.2.
Often followed by a further backward-elimination or stepwise procedure (either p-value or AIC based) on this already-reduced set, “to simplify the model further.”
Pitfall: This double selection (univariable filter + stepwise) compounds selection bias. The final model reflects two rounds of data-driven pruning with no correction for either.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
B.4 Missing data

Handle missingness by simple complete-case analysis at whichever stage it is convenient. Often a different subset at the screening stage (B.1) than at the final multivariable stage (B.3) is used without stating or checking the missing data mechanism.
Pitfall: No MAR/MCAR assessment; potential selection bias from differential missingness; inconsistent sample sizes across tables in the eventual report.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
B.5 Interactions and assumptions

Interactions between predictors are not considered. The workflow typically stops at main effects of the retained variables.
Proportional-hazards and functional-form assumptions are either not checked at all, or checked only informally (e.g., a single global test) after the model is already finalized; regularly without a plan for what to do if violated.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
B.6 Inference and reporting

Report the HRs, 95% CIs and p-values from the final reduced model as if the variables had been pre-specified, with no acknowledgment that they were chosen based on their own association with the outcome.
Pitfall: Standard errors, CIs and p-values from a selected model are invalid (i.e., anti-conservative); they do not reflect the extra uncertainty introduced by the selection step, and the retained effects are typically biased away from the null (“winner’s curse”).
Predictors are commonly described as independent prognostic factors based on this biased, selection-conditional model.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
B.7 Performance evaluation

Prediction performance (e.g., C-index, R^2-type measure) is computed on the same data used to select and fit the model (i.e., apparent performance), with no bootstrap or cross-validation correction for optimism.
Pitfall: Reported discrimination/calibration will be optimistically biased, sometimes substantially, because both variable selection and coefficient estimation used the same data without correction.

title: Statistical Analysis Plans: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
section: B.8 Why this workflow is problematic?
text:
B.8 Why this workflow is problematic?

Selection bias: univariable screening ignores confounding; a variable whose marginal association is null or reversed can be strongly predictive after adjustment (PMP22 here), and vice versa.
Biased effect estimates: retained variables’ hazard ratios tend to be inflated away from the null.
Invalid inference: Confidence intervalls and p-values from the final model do not account for the selection process.
Instability: which variables “survive” screening can change with small perturbations of the data (e.g., different bootstrap samples, slightly different cutoffs); this is usually not checked.
Multiple testing without correction: multiple univariable tests, then further tests within stepwise elimination, treated as if only one test had ever been performed.
Optimistic performance claims: apparent (non-validated) performance overstates real-world predictive ability.
Defeats the actual study aim: the workflow would drop PMP22 before it is ever assessed jointly with pT, pN, G and ER, which represents the specific scientific question this study was designed to answer.
No initial data analysis (IDA): unlike SAP A (A.2), this workflow proceeds directly to univariable screening without first checking data quality, coding, distributions, or the missing-data mechanism, which compounds all of the risks above and can itself introduce further undetected errors.
